_readme: Management and simulation numbers for Arch City and its Adventurer Guild. Gold amounts are whole numbers. Every day the party pays for food (see food: each fed member eats at the quality set for them in Manage Party) and for each housed member's night where they lodge (set per member in Manage Party): an inn (priced per person by inns), a residence the party owns (free), outside (see lodging), or on the road during quests (free: only food is paid). Nothing is paid on the road: a multi-day quest's food and lodging, and any payday on the trip, go on a tab (GameState.tab) settled at the next End Day, and contracts only lapse at End Day in the city. When negotiating, a companion values food & lodging at what the party would pay for the food and night an adventurer expects (lodging.expectedQuality). Party ranks come from renown (see ranks). Quests: stages is the enemy level range (an adventurer rank's levels; see adventurerRanks), count the enemy group size range, days how long the trip takes; gold and renown come from the quest's strength (see strength). companion.expectedWeeklyLoot is how much gold a candidate thinks a party of that rank earns per week; they use it to value a loot cut. simulation tunes the rival parties: the chance a party goes on a quest each day, its chance of success (the strength model's AI win chance, strength.winCurve, for its members counted as reference Adventurers of their level against the quest's enemies, clamped to minSuccess-maxSuccess), and what can go wrong. Each member levels up after a success with levelUpChanceOnSuccess x levelUpFalloff^(level - 1), so high levels come slowly. A party tries its promotion quest once it has the renown and at least a 50% chance. Experienced adventurers die less: each member's chance to be lost on a quest is multiplied by deathLevelFalloff^(level - 1) (at least minDeathFactor), and a party's wipe chance by the same factor for its average level. Parties recruit from the guild hall only adventurers within recruitLevelGap levels of their average (or anyone, when down to 2 members). New adventurers arrive at about the rate adventurers are lost, nudged toward targetAdventurers.
_partyRankWeights: How the rival parties are spread over the ranks when a new game starts, as relative weights (a rank's share is its weight over the total: D is 40/126, about 32%); there is always at least one A-rank party. After that, ranks follow renown (see ranks). Quest postings have their own weights (board.rankWeights).

ranks._comment: Party ranks. renown: the renown a party needs for each rank (D needs none): tuned so a party of 2 at D, 3 at C and 4 at B is promoted at about level 6, 11 and 16 (about 4 D quests, 11 C and 18 B). highestPromotion: the highest rank a promotion quest can reach (A for now: no party can be promoted to S; S's renown only matters for rivals that start at S). Reaching the next rank's renown puts a promotion quest of that rank on the board; completing it promotes the party. A party whose renown stays below its own rank's threshold for demotionDays days in a row drops a rank. Renown doesn't fade: a failed quest loses failedQuestRenown x that quest's renown, and each member who dies loses deathRenown x the quest's renown. A member who quits (unpaid wages, or Morale 0) costs quitRenownPerLevel x their level.

adventurerRanks._comment: An adventurer's own rank comes from their level: the level each rank starts at (below C is D). Quests of a rank have enemies of that rank's levels, and parties of a rank are made of adventurers of about that rank.

board._comment: The guild's quest board is shared with the rival parties, who take quests from it (see simulation). Each day up to maxPostsPerDay new quests are posted until it holds boardSize; each quest's rank is picked by rankWeights, relative weights (S 1, A 7, B 20, C 60, D 40, out of 128: a rank's share is its weight over the total), with nothing set aside for the player: in a slow week the rivals may take every quest at the player's rank. Quests vary: each rolls its enemy level and group size (see quests and threat), and pay is extra luck on the reward, so some quests are much better deals than others.

quests._comment: Per quest rank: stages (the enemy level range), count (the enemy group's size in threat points: enemies.json threat per unit, so a bandit is 1 and a rat 0.5, and weak types come in bigger packs), and days. Each quest rolls its level and its count independently; its total threat is count x strength(level) (see threat), and its gold and renown follow from that. Encounter size comes from the quest alone, never from the party that takes it. Quick Battle stages use the middle count of the rank their stage falls in.

strength._comment: Quest strength comes from the strength model (src/game/power.ts): the enemies a quest can be expected to field, valued as sqrt(effective HP x damage per turn) each and summed, so it grows with their stats and their number. A quest's par level is the level at which the reference party (four Adventurers of average B talent with the gear expected at that level, played by the AI) would win parWinRate of its battles against it; winCurve is the fitted AI win chance, 1 / (1 + e^-(a + b ln ratio)) for a party with power ratio `ratio` against the quest (tools/balance fits it). The usual gold for a quest is its strength x goldPerStrength (then x the board's pay roll); its renown is strength x renownPerStrength, then x (1 + renownPayFactor x (1 - pay roll)), so a quest paying 0.75 of the usual gold earns 1.25x the renown and one paying 1.35 earns 0.65x. Quest cards show the par level as skulls: half a skull at par level skulls.from up to ten at skulls.to, rising evenly in half steps (five white skulls, then red skulls over them).

food._comment: Food for every member the party feeds (the main character, slaves, and companions with food & lodging in their contract), set per member in Manage Party. Each day, a fed member costs that tier's pricePerPerson. Quality: poor 0, common 1, fine 2, luxury 3, compared with what they expect (lodging.expectedQuality, or lodging.slaveExpectedQuality for slaves) like a night's lodging: every fed member gains moraleAbovePerStep Morale for each step better than they expect and loses moraleBelowPerStep for each step worse. default is the tier for members nobody has set.

_inns: pricePerPerson: a night's lodging for one member assigned to the inn (Manage Party). drinksPerPerson / drinksMorale: a round of drinks for the whole party (once a day) costs drinksPerPerson per member and raises everyone's Morale by drinksMorale.

lodging._comment: Every day ends (End Day on the city screen) with a night for each housed member where they lodge, set per member in Manage Party: an inn, a residence the party owns (free; at most residences.capacity residents each), or the stables (stablesPerPerson). Members nobody has placed lodge at adventurerDefault (slaves: slaveDefault): 'outside' (the stables) or an inn (standard, highEnd, luxury); so do the residents of a residence that is sold. Night quality: the stables 0; the Sleeping Griffin or the Outer City House 1; the Silver Lantern or the Inner City Townhouse 2; the Gilded Crown or the Inner City Mansion 3. expectedQuality is the food and night quality adventurers expect (1: common food and an inn); slaves expect slaveExpectedQuality instead (0: poor food, the stables). Each night, every housed member (the main character, slaves, and companions with food & lodging in their contract) gains moraleAbovePerStep Morale for each step better than they expect, and loses moraleBelowPerStep for each step worse. Nights on the road during multi-day quests are free (food is still paid) and don't count.

residences._comment: Homes the party can buy and sell at the Estate Office (Inner City): one in the Outer City (key outer) and two in the Inner City (keys middle and inner; the keys are kept for old saves). Nights there are free and count as quality 1, 2 and 3 (see lodging). Each houses at most capacity residents, whatever its tier. The office buys a residence back for sellShare of its price.

churches._comment: The Church (Outer City) and the Central Church (Inner City). donations: give gold for a blessing on the party's next quest: every battle stat of everyone who goes +blessingPct% (one blessing at a time; a bigger donation replaces a smaller one, and it ends when that quest does). heal: pay gold to restore health Health to one member at once. After a healing, that member can't be healed again at either church for healCooldownDays days.

condition._comment: Health (0-100, not battle HP) and Morale (0-100) of party members. After a battle, Health drops by maxHealthLoss x the share of HP the unit lost at its lowest point (falling = the full amount). Below 100 Health a member is injured and can't go on quests; everyone recovers healthPerDay each night. A member whose Health reaches 0 dies (the main character is left at 1 instead). Morale changes: moralePerTurn for each battle turn (round) of a quest, for each member who went, moraleFailedQuest more if it fails, moralePerHealthLost per Health point lost to injuries, moraleMemberDied for everyone when a member dies. Food and lodging also move Morale every day (see food and lodging). New members start at startingMorale. Below lowMorale, companions and slaves lose lowMoraleRelationshipPerDay relationship each day; above highMorale they gain highMoraleRelationshipPerDay; a member at 0 Morale leaves the party (not the main character).

xp._comment: XP for a won quest. Every member who comes back gets the same as a day of training (schedule.trainingXp), plus an equal share of the quest's pool XP split among all of them (so smaller parties learn faster). The pool is pool.a x D^2 + pool.b x D + pool.c, where D is the quest's danger in skulls (0.5 to 10): 105 at half a skull, 560 at 4 skulls, 2480 at 10. The members' levels don't change it: the level-up cost curve (stats.json xpPerLevel) already makes easy quests worth little to veterans. Failed quests give no XP.

schedule._comment: What members who aren't on a quest do each day (Manage Party). recover: recovers recoverMultiplier x healthPerDay. training: trainingXp.perLevel x level + trainingXp.flat XP (22 at level 1, 70 at level 25). oddJobs: oddJobsGold gold. dayOff: dayOffMorale Morale. marketplace (anyone but mercenaries): sells up to marketplaceItemsPerDay items from the top of the Marketplace sale list, at their full value.

_mercenary: A mercenary is paid the larger of their fee (feePerLevel x level, paid up front when hired) and their cut (cutBase + cutPerLevel x level, % of the quest reward): if the cut of a won quest is worth more than the fee, they take the difference from the reward. Both x greed x talent price.

companion._patience: Offers a candidate hears before walking away: patience, plus 1 for every patiencePerRelationship relationship (renewals: 3 more at 90).
companion._comment: Releasing a companion before their term ends costs a payout: the smaller of releaseMinWeeks weeks of their compensation and releaseShareOfRemaining of their compensation for the days left. Compensation is base pay + expected loot cut + food & lodging (see offerValue). Free once the term has ended.

market._comment: The slave market. It holds between stock[0] and stock[1] slaves: each day dailySales of them are sold to other buyers (never below stock[0]), and on the shipmentWeekdays (day of the week, 0-6) a shipment of shipmentSize arrives (never above stock[1]). Prices are each slave's value (slave.priceBase + pricePerLevel x level x talent) times the price index, which drifts randomly by up to drift a day and is pulled toward (stockReference / stock)^0.5: scarce slaves cost more, a glut costs less. It stays within priceIndex. The market buys your slaves back for slave.sellBackShare of the current price. It doesn't take prisoners: they are registered at the city gate (see slave).

_slave: Prisoners (human foes who surrender) are registered at the city gate when the party comes back: turned in for bountyPerLevel x level gold (enemies killed pay nothing themselves: they drop loot, see enemies.json loot), or registered as the party's slave for a fee of its normal market value (priceBase + pricePerLevel x level x talent, at price index 1; talent is the slave's average stat growth rate: all C = 1, all S = 1.6, all F = 0.6) minus its bounty, so at a normal market enslaving and turning in come to the same. Every slave the party owns is taxed weeklyTaxShare of its normal market value each payday, along with companion wages; a slave whose tax can't be paid is seized by the city and goes to the slave market. Slaves have a relationship (like companions: quests together, nights better or worse than they expect, low Morale and missed upkeep move it) and Obedience (0-100). Market slaves start with obedienceMarket, registered captives with obedienceCaptive, both at startingRelationship. Each day Obedience rises by obedienceChangePerDay while relationship is at least obedienceRiseFrom, and falls by it while relationship is below obedienceFallBelow. Punishing a slave (Manage Party, once a day) adds punishObedience but costs punishRelationship.

combat._comment: Battle stats of party members drop by percentPer5 % for every 5 points of Morale below 100, and (slaves) of Obedience below 100. These multiply with each other and with the injury penalty (1/3 of missing Health).
